displayQuote: The unexamined life is not worth living

meta.title: Who really said "The unexamined life is not worth living"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes, Socrates said it — at his trial in 399 BC, recorded in Plato’s Apology 38a. But he wrote nothing; the words reach us only through Plato.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The unexamined life is not worth living'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Socrates, from his defense speech in Plato’s Apology (38a). The catch: Socrates wrote nothing, so we have it only via Plato.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: c. 470–399 BC · Athenian philosopher, as recorded by Plato
answer.sourceLine: The line is from Socrates’ defense speech at his trial in 399 BC, preserved in Plato’s Apology at section 38a. It is one of the best-documented quotations in the Western canon — with the important caveat that Socrates wrote nothing himself, so we have it only through his pupil Plato’s account.

source.heading: Plato, Apology 38a
source.excerpt: …if I say that it is the greatest good for a man to discuss virtue every day and those other things about which you hear me conversing and testing myself and others, for the unexamined life is not worth living for men, you will believe me even less.
trail: The passage is hosted at Perseus Digital Library, Apology 38a ↗ (Fowler’s English edition; Perseus hosts the Greek text separately).
The dictum is catalogued to Apology 38a5–6 by Wikipedia’s dedicated article ↗, which gives the Greek and transliteration.
Wikiquote’s Apology page ↗ lines up the Grube, Jowett and Tredennick/Tarrant renderings of the same sentence.
source.cutTag: ↑ the popular one-liner drops the argument it belongs to
source.excerptNote: Grube’s translation of Apology 38a. The Greek is ο δε ανεξέταστος βίος ου βιωτὸς ανθρώπῳ (ho de anexetastos bios ou biotos anthropoi) — literally “the unexamined life is not liveable for a man.”
source.rightsNote: The underlying text is ancient and long out of copyright; individual modern English translations (e.g. Grube’s) may themselves be under copyright, but the quote and its classical source are public domain.

author.name: Socrates
author.heading: About Socrates
author.bio: Socrates was a classical Athenian philosopher widely regarded as a founder of Western moral philosophy. Famous for the “Socratic method” of relentless questioning, he wrote nothing himself — almost everything we know of him comes through his pupils Plato and Xenophon. Tried on charges of impiety and corrupting the youth, he was sentenced to death and executed by hemlock in 399 BC.

misattribution.heading: Correctly Socrates — but watch the fine print
misattribution.intro: This is a rare case where the popular attribution is right. The confusions are subtler than a wrong name:

items.why: Because the line only exists in Plato’s Apology ↗, it is often filed under Plato. Within the text, though, the words are spoken by Socrates in his own defense — Plato is the author-narrator, not the speaker.

Self-help and motivational culture rebrand the line as a call to “find yourself.” As The Collector notes ↗, Socrates meant rigorous public philosophical inquiry into virtue, not private introspection or career planning.

misattribution.truthLine: Bottom line: genuinely Socrates, spoken at his trial and recorded in Plato’s Apology 38a ↗ — just remember it reaches us only through Plato’s pen.

context.heading: Why he said it
lead: Socrates spoke these words near the end of his trial in 399 BC, after the jury had found him guilty. Offered the chance to propose exile or to simply stop philosophizing as an alternative to death, he refused: to give up the daily examination of virtue, he argued, would empty life of its worth.
The famous clause is the culmination of that refusal — a defense of the philosophical life so uncompromising that he preferred execution to abandoning it.
detailsBody: Because Socrates left no writings, historians distinguish the “historical Socrates” from the character who appears in Plato’s dialogues. Whether the man actually uttered this exact sentence at his trial, or whether Plato crafted it as the perfect distillation of his teacher’s creed, cannot be settled — a limitation scholars call the “Socratic problem.”
What is certain is that the line is Plato’s record of Socrates, composed within a generation of the trial, and has been read as Socrates’ own for nearly 2,400 years.
